lesson.title: When Two Equations Describe the Same Line
lesson.summary: A dependent system is a consistent system in which the equations describe the exact same line, so every point on that line is a solution and there are infinitely many answers.
lesson.body:
A dependent system is a consistent system, so it has at least one solution, but instead of having exactly one like an independent system, it has infinitely many. This happens when the two equations are not really two different pieces of information at all; they describe the exact same line, just written differently, so any point that satisfies one equation automatically satisfies the other, no matter which point on the line you happen to pick. In that sense, a dependent system offers no additional restriction beyond what the first equation already provided on its own.

The contrast with independent systems from the previous section is worth stating plainly. Independent systems have lines with different slopes, crossing at one unique point. Dependent systems have lines with the same slope and the same y-intercept, meaning the two equations graph as a single line lying directly on top of itself, so every one of the infinitely many points on that line is shared by both equations. In a sense, a dependent system only looks like two equations; underneath, it is really just one piece of information written twice.

Consider the system 2x + y = 6 and 4x + 2y = 12. Notice that multiplying every term of the first equation by 2 gives exactly the second equation: 2(2x) + 2(y) = 2(6) produces 4x + 2y = 12. The two equations are equivalent, just scaled versions of one another. Confirm this algebraically using elimination: multiply the first equation by 2 to get 4x + 2y = 12, then subtract the second equation from it: (4x + 2y) - (4x + 2y) = 12 - 12, which simplifies to 0 = 0. That statement is always true, regardless of x and y, and reaching an identity like 0 = 0 while trying to eliminate a variable is the algebraic signal of a dependent system, in contrast with the false statement, like 0 = -6, that signals an inconsistent one.

Because there is no single answer, the solution set of a dependent system is described as every ordered pair satisfying the shared equation, for instance y = 6 - 2x. Any x-value produces a valid solution: at x = 0, y = 6, giving (0, 6); at x = 1, y = 4, giving (1, 4); at x = 3, y = 0, giving (3, 0). Check (3, 0) in both originals: 2(3) + 0 = 6 matches the first equation, and 4(3) + 2(0) = 12 matches the second, confirming it is a valid solution, just like every other point on that line, and the same check would succeed for any other point chosen along it.

Recognizing dependence quickly is a useful shortcut: whenever an elimination attempt collapses into 0 = 0, there is no need to keep solving for a single numeric answer, since the system's solution is the entire line described by either original equation, and reporting that line, rather than a single ordered pair, is the correct and complete answer for a dependent system. This same shortcut applies no matter which of the two equivalent equations you started from, since either one describes the identical line.
